models.text: The suite should implement elasticity theory, Cauchy stress equilibrium, Euler–Bernoulli and Timoshenko beam theories, curved beam formulations, von Mises yielding, Tresca yielding, thin-wall and thick-wall cylinder stress relationships, Lamé's equations, thermal expansion relationships, axial force equilibrium, Euler buckling, nonlinear beam-column equations and geometric stiffness formulations.

The suite should include lateral buckling models, upheaval buckling models, Hobbs-type thermal buckling formulations, nonlinear pipeline walking models, pipeline axial restraint models, combined loading collapse criteria, external pressure collapse models, burst pressure models, buckle propagation models, imperfections-based collapse analysis, nonlinear pipe–soil interaction, Coulomb friction and nonlinear seabed contact formulations.

The suite should implement Morison's equation, Airy and Stokes wave theories, drag and inertia loading, Keulegan–Carpenter correlations, Shields sediment mobility, pipe embedment models, seabed lateral stability models, free-span beam vibration, vortex shedding theory, Strouhal relationships, reduced velocity models, in-line and cross-flow VIV models, wake oscillator models and spectral fatigue models. The free-span assessment should distinguish direct wave loading, in-line VIV, cross-flow VIV and combined fatigue mechanisms, consistent with the scope of DNV-RP-F105.

The suite should implement conservation of mass, momentum and energy, Darcy–Weisbach pressure loss, Colebrook–White friction factor, Reynolds-number-dependent flow models, thermodynamic equations of state, Peng–Robinson and Soave–Redlich–Kwong equations of state, phase-equilibrium flash calculations, enthalpy balances, heat conduction, Newton's law of cooling, transient heat transfer and coupled fluid–wall–soil thermal models.

The suite should incorporate homogeneous equilibrium models, homogeneous non-equilibrium models, drift-flux models, Zuber–Findlay formulations, one-dimensional two-fluid models, six-equation and seven-equation multiphase formulations where appropriate, interfacial momentum transfer models, wall shear correlations, slip velocity correlations, flow-regime maps, Taitel–Dukler transition models, Beggs–Brill pressure-drop correlations, mechanistic slug-flow models, Kelvin–Helmholtz instability, slug initiation models, slug tracking methods, slug front propagation and terrain-induced severe slugging models.

models.group: Hydrate, wax, scale and deposition models
models.text: Hydrate modelling should include van der Waals–Platteeuw hydrate equilibrium theory, hydrate fugacity-based phase equilibrium, hydrate nucleation kinetics, classical nucleation theory, induction-time models, hydrate crystal growth, kinetic rate expressions, hydrate adhesion, deposition and agglomeration models, inhibitor thermodynamics and hydrate plugging risk formulations. Wax modelling should include wax appearance temperature, solid–liquid phase equilibrium, molecular diffusion, shear dispersion, wax crystallization, deposition and erosion/removal models. Scaling analysis should incorporate ionic activity models, precipitation equilibrium, saturation indices, aqueous speciation, nucleation, crystal growth and scale transport.

The suite should include electrochemical corrosion kinetics, Butler–Volmer relationships, Tafel kinetics, carbon dioxide corrosion correlations, corrosion mass-transfer models, erosion velocity correlations, particle-impact erosion models, wall-thickness deterioration, Paris–Erdogan crack propagation, fracture mechanics, failure assessment diagrams, corrosion defect remaining-strength models and structural reliability methods.

The suite should integrate finite-element structural models, finite-volume multiphase solvers, transient thermal models, nonlinear pipe–soil models, stochastic slugging and hydrate formation, Bayesian parameter calibration, Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation and coupled flow-assurance–structural-integrity analysis. High-fidelity alternatives should include Eulerian–Eulerian multiphase CFD, volume-of-fluid interface tracking, Eulerian–Lagrangian particle methods, CFD–DEM deposition models and fluid–structure interaction. Detailed models require verification of conservation, time-step convergence, grid convergence, closure sensitivity and validation against appropriate experimental or operational measurements.

subtitle: On-bottom stability, stress, buckling, installation, multiphase hydraulics, slugging, hydrates, corrosion and pipeline integrity.
ic: The initial conditions shall define the installed pipeline geometry, including route coordinates, seabed elevations, pipeline curvature, free spans, supports, crossings, burial depth and the initial pipe–soil contact configuration. The structural state shall include initial axial tension or compression, bending stresses, residual installation stresses and any known geometric imperfections.

For in-place structural analysis, the initial state shall represent equilibrium under submerged self-weight, internal contents, hydrostatic pressure, seabed support and sustained operating conditions. Thermal expansion and pipeline walking studies shall establish the initial pipe temperature, axial force, displacement and seabed friction state.

For hydraulic analysis, the pipeline shall be initialized with pressure, temperature, fluid composition, phase fractions, phase velocities, liquid holdup and flow regime along its length. Transient multiphase simulations shall use a consistent initial steady operating state or a specified non-equilibrium distribution.

For startup following shutdown, the initial condition shall include the cooled fluid temperature distribution, liquid accumulation, trapped gas distribution and shut-in pressure. Hydrate and wax studies shall initialize existing deposit thickness, wall temperature, fluid composition and dissolved inhibitor concentration where applicable.

Fatigue, corrosion and integrity simulations shall begin with the measured or assumed defect state, corrosion allowance consumption, crack sizes, accumulated fatigue damage and remaining wall thickness. Installation simulations shall use the pipeline configuration and lay tension corresponding to the selected installation stage.
bc: Hydraulic boundaries shall prescribe appropriate combinations of inlet flow rate, inlet pressure, inlet temperature, outlet pressure and downstream equipment characteristics. The selected conditions must be compatible with the flow formulation and must not overconstrain the hydraulic problem.

At the pipeline wall, the model shall impose no-penetration of fluid through an intact pipe wall, together with wall friction and thermal heat-transfer conditions. Thermal boundaries shall represent seawater temperature, insulation, burial, seabed temperature and heat transfer to surrounding media.

Structural boundaries shall represent end restraints, riser connections, pipeline-end terminations, spool flexibility, support reactions and imposed end displacements. At the seabed, the pipe shall interact through contact, friction, embedment, lateral resistance and uplift separation where applicable.

For on-bottom stability analysis, wave and current loads shall act along the exposed pipeline, with appropriate seabed friction and hydrodynamic interaction. For buckling, the model shall include axial restraint, thermal expansion, initial geometric imperfections and relevant seabed resistance.

Installation boundary conditions shall prescribe lay vessel motion, top tension, stinger support, departure angle and touchdown contact. Hydrate and wax modelling shall apply relevant wall deposition, heat-transfer, mass-transfer, nucleation and inhibitor-injection conditions.

Corrosion studies shall use appropriate internal fluid chemistry, wall exposure and external environmental conditions. Flow transients shall include controlled valve movement, pump changes, production ramps, shutdowns and restarts.

calibration: Calibration should use pipeline field operating records, high-pressure multiphase flow-loop measurements, pipe–soil interaction experiments, material tests, subsea surveys and documented pipeline integrity assessments.

Multiphase hydraulic models should be calibrated using measured pressure gradients, phase flow rates, liquid holdup, flow-regime observations and fluid property measurements. Interfacial friction, wall friction, phase slip and flow-regime transition parameters should be adjusted using representative flow-loop experiments, with particular attention to pipeline inclination and operating pressure.

Slugging models should be calibrated using measured slug frequency, slug length, slug velocity, liquid accumulation, slug arrival times and separator inlet measurements from instrumented flow facilities or field pipelines.

Hydrate formation and deposition models should use laboratory high-pressure hydrate-cell experiments, measured hydrate equilibrium conditions, induction times, nucleation observations, hydrate growth rates and deposition tests. Hydrate adhesion, wall capture and removal parameters should be informed by representative experiments rather than inferred solely from production data.
Wax and scale deposition models should be calibrated using measured precipitation characteristics, deposition experiments, temperature-dependent fluid properties and observed field deposition trends.

Hydrodynamic pipeline stability models should use wave-current flume experiments to inform drag, inertia and lift coefficients, including the effects of seabed clearance, pipe roughness and partial embedment.
Pipe–soil interaction models should be calibrated using lateral breakout tests, axial friction tests, penetration tests, cyclic pipe displacement experiments and site-specific geotechnical data.
Vortex-induced vibration models should use independent hydrodynamic experiments, measured vibration amplitudes, oscillation frequencies and fatigue loading histories.

Corrosion and erosion models should be calibrated against material coupon tests, laboratory flow-loop experiments, measured wall-thickness reduction, corrosion monitoring and relevant fluid chemistry measurements.
verification: Pipeline structural calculations should be verified using analytical benchmarks for internal pressure, external pressure, axial loading, thermal expansion, bending, buckling and combined loading.

Pipe finite-element models should undergo mesh refinement and nonlinear solution sensitivity studies covering lateral buckling, upheaval buckling, local collapse, propagation buckling and structural instability.
On-bottom stability calculations should be checked through force equilibrium, hydrodynamic load implementation and independently calculated benchmark cases.
Pipe–soil contact formulations should be verified for friction, penetration, lateral breakout, cyclic loading and contact separation.
Pipeline installation simulations should undergo discretization and convergence checks for overbend, sagbend, lay tension, curvature and vessel-induced loading.

Multiphase flow solvers should undergo conservation tests for mass, momentum and energy, numerical shock and discontinuity transport benchmarks, hydrostatic equilibrium checks, phase transport tests and spatial-temporal convergence studies.

Hydrate, wax and scale transport implementations should be checked for dimensional consistency, mass conservation, positivity of transported quantities, deposition bookkeeping and physically consistent coupling with temperature and flow.
Slug-tracking methods should be tested using prescribed moving-front problems, analytical transport cases where available, time-step refinement and controlled slug-propagation benchmarks.
Thermal calculations should be verified using steady and transient heat-transfer benchmarks, cooling problems and coupled fluid–wall temperature calculations.
Fatigue, corrosion and fracture calculations should be checked against independent reference solutions and known defect-assessment cases.
validation: Pipeline pressure, temperature and phase distribution predictions should be compared with independent operating data from instrumented field pipelines or suitable multiphase flow loops.
Slugging predictions should be evaluated against measured slug frequencies, lengths, velocities, liquid holdup and arrival times over multiple flow conditions.

Hydrate equilibrium predictions should be validated using independent laboratory phase-equilibrium measurements. Hydrate formation, deposition and plugging predictions require additional validation using representative kinetic and transport experiments.
Wax deposition and scale formation predictions should be assessed against independent laboratory deposition experiments and suitable field inspection or production records.
Pipeline on-bottom stability predictions should be compared against physical wave-current experiments and documented pipeline displacement observations.
Pipe–soil interaction predictions should be validated using independent pipe displacement and embedment tests representing the relevant seabed soils.
Free-span vibration and VIV fatigue predictions should be compared with instrumented pipe experiments or field vibration measurements.
Buckling and collapse predictions should be assessed using full-scale or representative structural experiments covering the relevant pipe geometries and material properties.
Corrosion, erosion and remaining-life predictions should be compared against inspection records acquired after the calibration period.

Validation should cover normal operation, shutdown, cooldown, restart, extreme environmental conditions and relevant abnormal operating scenarios. It should distinguish validation of flow assurance models from validation of structural integrity models.

geometry.text: Subsea pipelines, flowlines, tie-backs, pipeline crossings, free spans, pipe bends, riser bases, expansion loops, trench sections, buried pipelines, subsea connectors and complex pipeline routes.

geometry.cat: Conventional and universal CAD geometry formats
geometry.text: STEP, IGES, Parasolid, ACIS, DXF and supported DWG should be accepted for pipe solids, pipe sections, elbows, bends, tees, flanges, connectors, supports, crossings, coating layers and detailed pipe assemblies.

geometry.cat: Pipeline route and centreline geometry formats
geometry.text: CSV (.csv), TSV (.tsv), XYZ (.xyz), XML (.xml), JSON (.json), LandXML, GML, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, Shapefile and DXF polylines should be accepted where they contain valid pipeline coordinates, stationing, chainage, elevation, depth, pipe diameters, bend geometry or route connectivity. GeoTIFF and gridded seabed elevations should be supported to reconstruct the terrain beneath pipelines. The importer should preserve three-dimensional route coordinates, pipeline curvature, inclination, crossings, seabed clearance, embedment and connected pipeline branches.

The application should accept structured network models defining nodes, pipes, junctions, valves, tees, manifolds, fittings and equipment connectivity through documented XML, JSON or CSV schemas. An imported centreline may be combined with cross-sectional descriptions and coating geometry to reconstruct a three-dimensional pipe model.

geometry.cat: Finite-element and computational fluid geometry formats
geometry.text: Nastran BDF, Abaqus INP, ANSYS CDB, Gmsh MSH, MED, UNV, VTK/VTU, Exodus, CGNS, SU2 and OpenFOAM polyMesh should be accepted for compatible structural, buckling, thermal and CFD models. Imported CFD meshes must represent suitable internal flow volumes rather than only the external pipe surface.

STL, OBJ, PLY, GLB, LAS/LAZ, E57, XYZ bathymetry, GeoTIFF, ESRI ASCII Grid, gridded multibeam surveys and inspection-derived point clouds should be supported for pipeline free spans, crossings, seabed embedment, pipe deformation, corrosion-defect geometry and as-laid pipeline reconstruction. Inspection datasets with no explicit spatial geometry would require additional mapping before becoming usable geometric inputs.
